claims.text: Entropic stabilization of the multi-element HEA matrix promotes selective oxidation of reactive alloying elements.
The selectively oxidized reactive elements are slower-diffusing elements.
Selective oxidation produces a continuous oxide film.
The resulting oxide film is adherent and self-healing.
The initial HEA is homogeneous and has multiple alloying elements distributed uniformly.
High-temperature exposure in an oxygen-rich atmosphere forms a thin, continuous, adherent oxide scale on the HEA surface.
The protective scale may consist of Al2O3, Cr2O3, or a mixed oxide.
High configurational entropy lowers diffusion rates in HEAs.
Sluggish diffusion enhances selective oxidation of reactive elements.
Entropic stabilization and sluggish diffusion cause rapid formation of a protective oxide layer.
The protective oxide remains stable and self-healing during high-temperature exposure.
The protective oxide reduces further oxidation relative to alloys lacking multi-element entropic stabilization.
Relative to a conventional-alloy baseline, the HEA will form a thinner oxide scale.
Relative to the baseline, the HEA oxide scale will be more uniform and less porous.
Relative to the baseline, the HEA will have lower oxidation weight gain and better long-term stability.
Conventional alloys lacking multi-element entropic stabilization typically form thicker, less adherent, and more porous oxide scales.
The proposed mechanism is applicable when selective oxidation and sluggish diffusion predominate under high-temperature oxidation conditions.
Changes in oxygen partial pressure, extreme temperatures, or composition outside the designed HEA system may alter the oxidation behavior.

contradictions.description: The baseline is described as having similar overall oxidation rates, while the prediction requires the HEA to show lower overall oxidation and lower weight gain than that baseline.
